# QCSchema adapter test corpus

Every case is a directory `tests/fixtures/<case>/` holding `document.json`
(the exact QCSchema document) and `meta.json` (`{outcome, expected, family,
driver, raw_sha256, ...generator}`). `test_corpus.py` discovers every
directory under here that contains both files and asserts the adapter's
actual outcome against `meta.json["expected"]`.

## Real Psi4 runs (`energy_*`, `gradient_*`, `hessian_*`, `optimization_*`, `failed_job`)

Generated by actually running Psi4 through qcengine — not hand-authored —
in a dedicated conda environment (`tckdb_qcschema_psi4`, not `tckdb_env`):

```
conda create -n tckdb_qcschema_psi4 -c conda-forge python=3.11 psi4 qcengine geometric qcelemental=0.51.2
```

Its exact package set is pinned in `ENVIRONMENT.lock.txt`
(`conda list --explicit` output; `conda create -n <env> --file ENVIRONMENT.lock.txt`
reproduces it). Versions actually used: Psi4 1.11, qcengine 0.51.0,
qcelemental 0.51.2, geometric 1.1.1.

System: water (H2O), standard experimental geometry (r(OH)=0.9584 Å,
angle=104.45°), HF/STO-3G — a cheap level chosen only to make the run fast;
nothing about the mapping logic this corpus exercises depends on method or
basis.

Each v1 document is the direct `qcengine.compute(...)` /
`qcengine.compute_procedure(..., "geometric")` result, serialised with
`.json()`. Each `_v2` sibling is `result.convert_v(2)` on that same v1
result — qcelemental's own family-conversion method — then serialised the
same way. `energy`/`gradient`/`hessian` are three separate `AtomicInput`
jobs on the same input geometry (driver `energy`/`gradient`/`hessian`
respectively); `optimization` is a `geometric`-driven `OptimizationInput`
starting from the same geometry.

`failed_job` is `qcengine.compute(...)` on the same molecule with
`model.basis="definitely-not-a-real-basis-set"`, `raise_error=False`. The
result is **not** a `success=false` `AtomicResult` — it is a genuine
`FailedOperation` (fields: `id`, `input_data`, `success`, `error`,
`extras`; no `schema_name`/`schema_version`/`driver`/`model` at all).
Measuring this shape directly is why `reader.py` checks `success` on the
raw parsed dict before attempting any family-specific class validation —
see the module docstring there.

## Identity-resolution case

- **`identity_unavailable`** — `energy_v1.json` reused verbatim (no
  `molecule.identifiers.smiles`), imported with `smiles_arg: null` in
  `meta.json` so `test_corpus.py` calls the mapper with no `--smiles`
  equivalent. Exercises the "no SMILES source at all" refusal and, via
  mutation, the "never perceive from 3D" invariant: a build that fell back
  to geometry perception when SMILES is absent would turn this refusal
  into a (wrong) success.

## Hand-derived cases

Each is one exact, documented edit to a copy of a real fixture above
(`energy_v1.json` unless noted), made with `qcelemental` still installed
so the edited document is re-validated as a real `Molecule`/`AtomicResult`
(not merely well-formed JSON). **Not** run through any real ESS — labelled
here as hand-derived, never as a Psi4 result.

- **`ghost_atom`** — `molecule.real` set to `[false, true, true]` (the
  oxygen atom marked a ghost/dummy atom, as counterpoise-style inputs do).
- **`two_fragments`** — a fourth atom (He) appended 50 bohr from the water
  molecule, with `molecule.fragments` **explicitly** set to
  `[[0, 1, 2], [3]]` (plus matching `fragment_charges`/
  `fragment_multiplicities`). Measured: qcelemental does not run
  distance-based auto-fragmentation on a plain `Molecule(**dict)`
  construction — omitting `fragments` on this same 4-atom geometry still
  validates as one fragment covering all four atoms — so the two-fragment
  claim has to be stated, exactly as a real multi-fragment QCSchema
  document (a supersystem or counterpoise input) would state it. The
  appended atom's mass is set to qcelemental's own tabulated He-4 mass
  (not a truncated literal), so this fixture exercises only the fragment
  count, not `nonstandard_mass`.
- **`nonstandard_mass`** — `molecule.masses[0]` (oxygen, `mass_numbers[0]`
  left at the standard 16) changed from the tabulated 15.99491461957 amu to
  15.0 — a corrupted/garbage mass on an otherwise ordinary atom, not a
  genuine isotope substitution (which would also change `mass_numbers`).
- **`non_integer_multiplicity`** — `molecule.molecular_multiplicity`
  changed from `1.0` to `2.5`. QCSchema types both `molecular_charge` and
  `molecular_multiplicity` as `float` (measured against the pinned
  `Molecule` model); TCKDB's species identity requires an integer, so a
  genuinely fractional value — not merely a float-typed 1.0 or 2.0 — is
  refused.
- **`family_drift`** — starting from `energy_v2.json` (which carries
  `input_data`, so dispatches to family v2 by shape), `schema_version` is
  changed from `2` to `1` with `schema_name` left at
  `"qcschema_atomic_result"`. This is the version-trap case itself: the
  document's shape says v2, but its own declared pair is not valid for
  that family (v2's valid `schema_version` is `2` for both record kinds).
- **`family_drift_v1_shape`** — the mirror-image edit, starting from
  `energy_v1.json` (no `input_data`, so dispatches to family v1 by
  shape): **both** `schema_version` (`1` -> `2`) **and** `schema_name`
  (`"qcschema_output"` -> `"qcschema_atomic_result"`) are changed, so the
  document ends up declaring v2's entire pair, not just one field of it
  (see `meta.json`'s `edit`, which already stated this correctly -- this
  paragraph previously didn't). That second field is not incidental: a
  reader that gates on "does the declared pair look internally
  self-consistent?" rather than strictly on shape would see a document
  declaring a fully matched v2 `(schema_name, schema_version)` pair and
  could be tempted to trust it -- exactly the failure the version trap
  warns about (`reader.py`'s module docstring: family is decided by shape
  alone, `input_data`'s presence, never by anything the document itself
  claims about its own version). Changing `schema_version` alone would
  already refuse (a v1-shaped document declaring `schema_version: 2`
  fails the version check on its own), so it would not by itself catch a
  reader that only checks `schema_name` for family-consistency and
  tolerates a mismatched version when the name still passes. Declaring
  the complete, self-consistent v2 pair is what forces shape to be the
  *only* thing that can decide family, regardless of which of the two
  declared fields a weaker implementation happens to check.

  Both `family_drift` cases refuse the same code, but for different
  reasons a reader that dispatches from the integer (or from the
  declared pair's own internal consistency) would get backwards in
  different ways -- `family_drift` would be dispatched to the wrong
  family and then simply fail generic class validation
  (`document_invalid`, not the specific code), while
  `family_drift_v1_shape` would be dispatched to family v2 by the
  integer/pair and then fail v2's `input_data`-required validation the
  same way. Keeping both is what makes "family taken from the integer"
  an observable mutation in both directions rather than one.

## Regenerating

```
conda run -n tckdb_qcschema_psi4 python gen_fixtures.py <tmp_raw_dir>
conda run -n tckdb_qcschema_psi4 python gen_hand_fixtures.py <tmp_raw_dir> <tmp_hand_dir>
python finalize_fixtures.py   # assembles tests/fixtures/<case>/{document.json,meta.json}
```

(The three generator scripts are not committed to the repo — they are
one-off corpus-authoring tools, not part of the adapter or its test
suite. Regenerating the corpus means recreating them from this README's
description, or asking for them again.)
